hypothesis: Feruloylagmatine (KEGG C18325) is increased or characteristic in 12-month-old infants relative to 5-month-old infants.
rationale: Searches returned no study - human, animal, or in vitro - that measured feruloylagmatine in infant stool, urine, or plasma, and none that compared it between milk-fed and complementary-fed / older infants. What the literature does establish is compositional/chemical: feruloylagmatine is a plant hydroxycinnamic acid amide (phenolamide) characterized in cereals (winter wheat crowns, barley/beer phenolamide profiles, rice HCAA biosynthesis) and in some medicinal plants, i.e. a dietary/exogenous compound rather than an endogenous infant metabolite. Because cereal-based complementary foods are typically introduced between ~4-6 months and are staples by 12 months, a purely dietary-exposure argument predicts higher levels at 12 months than at 5 months, when intake is still largely milk-based. A secondary, also indirect, route is chemical/microbial: cereal-derived ferulic acid reaching the colon plus agmatine generated by the widely distributed microbial arginine decarboxylases could in principle yield feruloyl-agmatine conjugates, but no study was found demonstrating this conjugation in the human gut. Infant fecal-metabolome studies spanning the complementary feeding window (e.g. the 'Nourish to Flourish' 4/9/12-month study; longitudinal 1-24 month profiling) show broad diet-driven metabolome shifts with solid food introduction but do not report this specific compound. This is therefore generic, pathway/food-composition-level reasoning with no feature+group-specific study, which maps to a confidence score of 1 rather than 2. No contradicting evidence was found, so -1 is not appropriate; relevant contextual literature was found, so 0 is not appropriate.

evidence.title: Antifungal Compound, Feruloylagmatine, Induced in Winter Wheat Exposed to a Low Temperature
evidence.study_population: Winter wheat (Triticum aestivum cv. Chihokukomugi) crowns; plant study
evidence.relevance: Primary study isolating feruloylagmatine from a cereal plant, supporting a cereal/plant-food dietary origin - the basis for expecting higher exposure once grain-based complementary foods dominate the diet at 12 months. Indirect: no human or infant data.

evidence.title: Identification of hordatines and other phenolamides in barley (Hordeum vulgare) and beer by UPLC-QTOF-MS
evidence.study_population: Barley grain and beer samples (food chemistry)
evidence.relevance: Documents hydroxycinnamoyl-agmatine phenolamides (feruloyl/coumaroyl agmatines and their hordatine dimers) as constituents of barley and barley-derived foods/beverages, i.e. plausible dietary sources of feruloylagmatine in a cereal-containing diet. Indirect, non-infant.

evidence.title: Hydroxycinnamic acid amides in rice: biosynthesis, distribution, function, and implication for crop development
evidence.study_population: Rice (Oryza sativa); review of plant biosynthesis
evidence.relevance: Corroborates that hydroxycinnamoyl-agmatine amides are produced by staple cereals including rice, a very common first complementary food, supporting the dietary-exposure rationale for a 12-month increase. Review-level and non-human.

evidence.title: Adaptation of the infant gut microbiome during the complementary feeding transition
evidence.study_population: Healthy infants sampled before solids (~4 months), at 9 months, and at 12 months ('Nourish to Flourish' pilot)
evidence.relevance: Primary human infant study showing substantial microbiome and paired LC-MS metabolite change across exactly the 4/5- to 12-month window, establishing that diet-derived fecal metabolite shifts occur in this interval - but it does not report feruloylagmatine, so it supports plausibility only, not the specific feature.

evidence.title: Effects of Whole-Grain and Sugar Content in Infant Cereals on Gut Microbiota at Weaning: A Randomized Trial
evidence.study_population: 4-7 month old Spanish infants receiving infant cereals as first weaning foods (RCT)
evidence.relevance: Confirms that cereal (including whole-grain) products are among the first and predominant complementary foods in infancy, the exposure route by which cereal phenolamides such as feruloylagmatine would rise after ~5 months. Does not measure the metabolite.

evidence.title: Diversity and distribution of amino acid decarboxylase enzymes in the human gut bacteria—a bioinformatics investigation
evidence.study_population: Bioinformatic survey of prevalent human gut bacterial genomes
evidence.relevance: Shows arginine decarboxylase (agmatine-producing) is encoded by ~60% of common gut bacteria, providing the agmatine moiety needed for any in-gut conjugation with cereal-derived ferulic acid. Purely theoretical support; conjugation to feruloylagmatine in the gut was not demonstrated in any retrieved source.

caveats: No literature was found on feruloylagmatine in any human biofluid, let alone in infants, so the directional expectation rests entirely on food-composition logic (cereal phenolamide + cereal-heavy diet at 12 months). Annotation risk is material: at the level of an untargeted aqueous-phase feature, C15H22N4O3 conjugates and other phenolamides/guanidino compounds are near-isobaric or isomeric (e.g. coumaroyl/feruloyl polyamine conjugates, hordatine fragments), so MS2/standard confirmation would be needed before treating this as feruloylagmatine. If the cohort's complementary foods are not cereal- or plant-based (e.g. predominantly dairy/meat purees), the dietary rationale weakens substantially. Also, absorbed hydroxycinnamates are extensively hydrolysed/conjugated (sulfation, glucuronidation) and colonic microbiota degrade ferulic acid, so the intact amide may be a poor and variable readout of intake.
